https://english.news.cn/europe/20260725/.text: Romania shoots down 2nd drone violating airspace in 2 days BUCHAREST, July 25 (Xinhua) -- Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Saturday that Romania had shot down another drone after it violated the country's airspace, marking the second such incident in two days. The drone was downed about 10 km west of Sfantu Gheorghe in central Romania, Dan said. Romania's Ministry of National Defense said in a statement that its radar surveillance systems detected an unauthorized drone entering the east European country's national airspace and flying in the border area with Ukraine. "Two F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft of the Romanian Air Force intercepted the air target and executed standard identification and neutralization procedures. The drone was safely shot down in an unpopulated area near the border," the ministry said. It added that the drone was brought down by the same pilot who had shot down the Shahed drone in Buzau County on Friday. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily

https://spacedaily.com/d-astronomers-hav.text: In 1981, astronomers stumbled onto what looked, at the time, like the largest hole ever found in the universe. It didn’t turn up in a telescope. It turned up on a bar chart. Four astronomers, Robert Kirshner, Augustus Oemler Jr, Paul Schechter and Stephen Shectman, published a four-page letter in The Astrophysical Journal with a question mark in the title. Between them they had measured redshifts for 133 galaxies across three small patches of northern sky. Each patch was about a degree and a half wide, and each sat some 35 degrees from the other two. Redshift stands in for distance, so plotting those 133 numbers gives you a crude map of depth. Their plot should have humped up in the middle, where the survey was most sensitive. Instead, it sagged. In the 6,000 kilometre-per-second band centred on 15,000, only one of the 133 galaxies was sitting there. Their own maths had asked for about twenty-five. Doubts from the authors themselves The letter asks it outright: was the histogram “a profound fact about the universe or a statistical accident”? Kirshner and his co-authors had their doubts too. They noted that they had drawn the boundaries of the gap after seeing where the points fell, which flatters any probability you calculate afterwards. Their own supporting evidence, by their own admission, was slim. Three narrow beams had been sampled, and the claim on the table was that the enormous wedge of space between those beams was empty too. Nor were they the first to find a hole. Laird Thompson and Stephen Gregory reported voids of their own in 1978, the same year a separate Estonian team found some independently. They later placed the Boötes work in the second wave of redshift surveys . What the 1987 follow-up found The follow-up settled it. Kirshner’s group went back and measured 240 bright galaxies in the region between their three original fields, and not one had a redshift between roughly 12,000 and 19,000 kilometres per second. A uniformly populated universe predicts 31 galaxies in that slice, as documented by the astronomer Greg Bothun in a review of the observations hosted by Caltech’s extragalactic database. The same survey shrank the void’s claimed size. Thompson and Gregory put the remeasured volume at about a third of the figure advertised in the 1981 title. That leaves a radius near 34 megaparsecs per unit of the Hubble parameter, which lands somewhere around 150 million light-years depending on whose expansion rate you prefer. Modern estimates of the diameter run from 250 to 330 million light-years, and the centre sits roughly 700 million light-years from here. BBC Science Focus makes the scale legible: the Milky Way would fit inside the region billions of times over. Sixty galaxies, arranged in a tube Astronomer Greg Aldering supplied the line that made the void famous. From inside it, he said, we “wouldn’t have known there were other galaxies until the 1960s”. Edwin Hubble sorted that out in the 1920s, so Aldering is docking us four decades of cosmology. His comparison appears in a post on NASA Goddard’s Blueshift blog . The post runs the sum behind the headline number too. Take one galaxy per ten million light-years as a rough density for the general universe, apply it to this volume, and you should find about 2,000. Surveys have found around 60. That figure comes from a rule of thumb, so treat it gently, but even reasonable fiddling with the assumptions doesn’t move the ratio much. The 60 are not scattered evenly, either. They sit along a rough tube running through the middle, which is one reason astronomers suspect the region was assembled from smaller voids that merged, the way soap bubbles combine when the film between them gives out. How Aldering’s own data made the void ordinary Does the emptiness amount to an anomaly? Aldering spent years combing infrared satellite data for anything hiding in there. Bothun’s review records the haul: 53 galaxies inside the boundaries Kirshner’s team had drawn, plus a redefined density profile. That left the region’s overall characteristics looking fairly typical of voids turning up in other surveys. Aldering was the one who made the void sound so strange in the first place. He also helped show that it is a fairly ordinary void, just an unusually large one. Entry number 88 Last year, a group led by Rosa Malandrino at the Institut d’Astrophysique de Paris published a Bayesian catalogue of 100 high-significance voids in the nearby universe. They built it by running a void-finding algorithm across fifty simulated reconstructions of the cosmic neighbourhood, then keeping only the underdensities that showed up again and again. Boötes made the cut. It is entry 88, radius 39.5 megaparsecs over h, plus or minus 2.9. Voids fill most of the volume of the cosmos, and because they hold so little matter, their growth is governed almost entirely by cosmic acceleration. That makes them useful for testing dark energy and gravity at the largest scales. All of that leaves the Boötes Void in a strange position. Its emptiness is the ordinary condition of the universe, sampled faithfully across three hundred million light-years. We are the anomaly, perched in a bright crowded filament, doing our sums as though that were the normal way to live. https://aa.com.tr/en/eurasia/poland-scra.text: RSS Diary Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 Eurasia Poland scrambles military aircraft as Russia launches strikes on Ukraine 'These actions are of a preventive nature and are aimed at securing airspace and its protection,' says Polish Army Diyar Güldoğan 20 August 2026 • Update : 20 August 2026 WASHINGTON DC Poland activated military aircraft and placed ground-based air defense and radar systems on heightened readiness early Thursday in response to Russian long-range aviation activity targeting Ukraine, the Polish Army said. "In accordance with applicable procedures, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, through the Air Operations Center - Air Component Command, has activated the necessary forces and resources at its disposal," it said on the US social media platform X. Poland also placed its ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance assets on a heightened state of readiness. "These actions are of a preventive nature and are aimed at securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions," it added. http://www.hongkongherald.com/news/27931.text: EU Parliament urges sanctions over Hong Kong jailing of activists CN 17 Sep 2026, 18:49 GMT+10 (AFP) - The European Parliament on Thursday called for sanctions against Chinese and Hong Kong officials over the imprisonment of three activists in Hong Kong for organizing vigils for those killed in the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown. The prison sentences of up to seven years imposed this month on Lee Cheuk-yan, 69; Chow Hang-tung, 41; and Albert Ho, 74, drew international condemnation. European Parliament members overwhelmingly backed a nonbinding resolution condemning the sentences, which were issued under a national security law Beijing imposed on Hong Kong in 2020 following massive pro-democracy protests. Hong Kong and Macau were the only places on Chinese soil that allowed public mourning for those killed on June 4, 1989, when Beijing sent troops and tanks to crush protests calling for political reform in and around the capital's Tiananmen Square. But public commemorations have effectively been banned in the cities in recent years. The lawmakers called on the European Commission to use the bloc's human rights sanctions regime "against all responsible HK (Hong Kong) and PRC (China) officials." The resolution said the commission should also begin working toward the "suspension" of Hong Kong's status in the World Trade Organization, where it is a member separate from China. "Hong Kong has become a tool of Beijing's foreign policy, a gateway for circumventing EU sanctions against Russia and, tragically, a place where there is no longer any space for democracy," conservative Slovak lawmaker Miriam Lexmann told the European Parliament. https://www.express.co.uk/news/uk/226147.text: Home News UK The UK is vulnerable, experts have said (Image: Getty) Experts have warned that the UK is complacent about the prospect of a Russian attack and ill-equipped to repel it. Commodore (Ret’d) Steve Prest, a RUSI Associate Fellow, said that the risk of a war against Russia is the greatest it has been since the height of the Cold War, and, “in many ways, certainly a confrontation” with Moscow is already taking place. Attacks on the UK mainland is an “entirely plausible situation”, he added, if Britain gets “caught up in a NATO conflict”. The former Royal Navy man fears that Britons are not fully cognisant of the possibility of war, akin to the attitude of the Government and public before the COVID -19 pandemic. He mentioned Ukraine , Gaza, Iran and African countries. “War has found them and it's pretty awful,” Commodore Prest said, “and we do have this sort of complacency, I think, and I'd include myself in this, that it could never happen here. Not in our leafy suburbs, or whatever. But the reality is it could." Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT The expert said the UK needs to “have a really hard think about our integrated missile defence”. A recent Sky documentary — Wargame — depicted a Russian attack on London and emphasised Britain’s limited capabilities. Russian drones could also “start finding their way, not into military facilities, but into our civil society in mainland UK”, Commodore Prest suggested. He asked: "And what would we do about it? What could we do about it?” The UK needs a “layered integrated air and missile defence system, which defends our highest vulnerability and highest priority targets or central targets from external attack with a sophisticated commander control system that can allocate and make real-time decisions”, the expert said. But he highlighted that it would not be possible to install a system “that shoots down everything that might possibly be locked at the UK at any time in the next 30 years”. “This isn't the Avengers,” Commodore Prest added. “You know, there's a degree of realism one has to apply.” Get exclusive defence news and analysis from our experts and more I would like to receive emails from the Daily Express featuring our latest products, services, offers, and promotions from across the Reach Plc family . Britain should, however, should “have done and be doing more than we are”, he says. Improvements will “take a significant degree of investment”, he added, “and there are models out there which would allow us to move more quickly”. It comes as the Chancellor was yesterday accused of putting politics ahead of the nation’s security in his Budget . John Healey did not outline how Britain would spend 3% of its GDP on defence. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Former soldier and Conservative veterans minister, Tobias Ellwood, said conventional warfare is no longer prevalent and Russia would seek to do damage from afar. “We saw that with the cyber attack on Jaguar Land Rover, the mapping of undersea cables,” he added. “These are all the things that are very likely to happen in the next few years. So this is why we must really need to understand how conflict is changing. This idea that Russia's going to attack by landing their forces on a Scottish island or off Dover — that's not the way warfare is today.” Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Drones could be launched off a Russian shadow fleet trawler, Mr Ellwood suggested. Undersea cables could also be clipped, and there could be another large-scale cyber attack. The veteran is also concerned about the possibility the UK’s gas supplies could be disrupted. “We just have nine days’ gas supplies,” he cautioned. "These are the sort of clever things that, I'm afraid, Russia and other countries are getting very good at,” Mr Ellwood said, “and we are very, very open and very, very, very prone to be disrupted from." It's the massive disinformation campaign, which already exists. It's assassinations, this is what they do well in Russia, when somebody goes against the system, swims against the tide. "And so the Russian mindset is very, very simple, and they will target Britain, our homeland directly, to sow societal discord, to disrupt our economy, and to challenge our politics, to get us arguing with each other. That's what they want. It's not about securing any land, any territory, in the old traditional sense. That's not what modern warfare is about."
